answer:
I found no email in which Jeff Skilling wrote about starting an Enron-owned airline.

- **His own mail:** I counted emails from his Enron addresses (jeff.skilling@enron.com, ken.skilling@enron.com, skilling@enron.com, mark.skilling@enron.com) and his yahoo address. None contained "airline", "airlines", "airplane", "aircraft" or "jet". A second count on jeff.skilling@enron.com alone found nothing for "aviation", "airline", "air carrier", "flights" or "plane".
- **Phrase searches:** Searches for "Enron Airlines", "start an airline" and "buy an airline" returned nothing relevant.
- **One aviation lead:** A calendar entry dated 2000-11-03 from Steven Kean reads "Mtg. w/Skilling and Hamad re Accelerator" – "meeting in Skilllings office re aviation". It has no body text and no sender statement from Skilling. It says nothing about an airline, so I can't tie it to an airline plan.
- **Other airline-related mail:** None of it is Skilling writing about an airline.
  - A November 2000 note from John Allario proposed a call option contract on passenger travel tickets to cut the $30 to $40 million Enron pays each year in airline travel.
  - A September 2000 white paper by Fred Philipson suggested using EOL as a non-vessel-owning common carrier for air cargo capacity.
  - A December 2000 overview of the Continental relationship says Enron Global Markets was exploring weather derivatives, plastics hedging and on-line jet swaps with Continental.

  Skilling wrote none of these. They concern trading and hedging, not owning an airline.

The store holds only 28 emails from jeff.skilling@enron.com (January 2000 to August 2001). The idea may never have been put in writing, or it may sit in mail the store doesn't hold.

Subject: Mtg. w/Skilling and Hamad re Accelerator
From: steven.kean@enron.com
To: nobody listed
Cc: nobody listed
Date: 2000-11-03meeting in Skilllings office re aviation

I thought perhaps Enron could develop a call option contract on passenger 
travel tickets, which would help reduce the approximate $30 to $40 million 
Enron pays each year in corporate airline travel.   If Enron could 
successfully develop this contract with Continental, we could roll it out to 
other large corporations and airlines.  After corporate acceptance, the ATC 
may then become a widely traded contract.

I recently authored a white paper, giving some background on the air cargo 
business for Enron Net Works.  In the paper, I identified the hurdles we 
would need to overcome in order to create a market for trading air cargo 
capacity futures, none of which were deemed insurmountable.  I further 
suggested that Enron could approach this business by leveraging EOL to act as 
a non vessel owning common carrier, trading physical capacity while readying 
the market (and ourselves!) for financial trading.

Additionally, Enron has a strong relationship with Continental's Fuel 
Management company.  Specifically, Enron has been hedging Continental's crude 
oil over the past 2+ years.  Value to Enron has been over $9 million; value 
to Continental has been over $45 million since 1999.  Enron Global Markets is 
currently exploring several other business propositions with Continental 
Airlines in the following areas of financial risk management:  weather 
derivatives, plastics hedging, and on-line jet swaps.  Enron Energy Services 
is exploring an energy (electric commodity) deal with Continental as well.
